I am 70 years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou County for 40 years. I finished high school back in my youth, so I can read the labels on fertilizer bags and I understand what the extension technician tells me when he comes to the village. But I also know that book knowledge is only worth something if it matches what I see with my own eyes in my fields. My farm is 7.7 mu, which is not large but it is enough to feed my family of five if I manage it carefully. I divide it into two parts: 5 mu I keep for the wheat-maize double-cropping system, and the remaining 2.7 mu I plant to cotton. I do it this way because cotton prices have been unpredictable, and I do not want to gamble the whole farm on it. Wheat and maize give me grain security and a steady baseline.

For the winter wheat that is already in the ground, I planted it last October after rotary tilling the soil to break up the compaction from the previous maize crop. I used an improved wheat variety at 20 kg per mu. Before planting, I applied 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base dressing — that gave me roughly 7 kg each of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Now that spring is here, I will irrigate three times: once at green-up in late March, once at jointing in mid-April, and once during grain filling in mid-May. Pumping water from the well costs electricity, and I have calculated that three irrigations is the right balance for my soil — four would waste money without adding much yield. At jointing, I will topdress with 25 kg of urea per mu, which adds about 11.5 kg of nitrogen. My total nitrogen for wheat comes to about 18 kg per mu. I will spray pesticide twice: a herbicide in early spring to control weeds, and a fungicide at flag-leaf stage if I see any yellow rust spots. Based on last year's result and the soil moisture this spring, I am targeting 500 kg per mu.

For summer maize, I will sow hybrid seed immediately after wheat harvest in mid-June. The turnaround is only six or seven days, so there is no time for ploughing — I will plant no-till into the wheat stubble. I have 2 kg of hybrid maize seed per mu ready. At planting, I put down 40 kg of compound fertilizer per mu, and at the big trumpet stage I will topdress with 15 kg of urea. That brings my total to about 16 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. Maize here does not need as much water as wheat; I will irrigate twice, once at seedling stage if the soil is dry, and once at tasseling. Two pesticide applications: a pre-emergence herbicide and one spray for Asian corn borer if I see moth activity in July. I expect about 550 kg per mu, which is what I have averaged the last three years.

For cotton on my 2.7 mu plot, I will plough the field in mid-April to warm up the soil and break the weed roots. I plant hybrid cotton at 3 kg of seed per mu. Cotton is tricky — too much nitrogen and the plants grow tall but drop their bolls. I apply 35 kg of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, and 10 kg of urea at first flowering. That is about 15 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu total. I irrigate twice: at flowering and at peak boll stage. Cotton bollworm is the main enemy here, so I will spray three times — once at squaring, once at flowering, and once at boll opening if I see worms. I am hoping for 280 kg per mu, which is realistic if the early summer rain is normal.

I always keep my input costs in mind. Fertilizer prices went up again this year, and every yuan I spend on the pump is a yuan I cannot spend on hired labor at harvest. Still, I would rather apply a little too much fertilizer than risk losing yield. A bad harvest is a disaster for my family; wasting a few kilograms of urea is just a cost I can absorb.
